about: Declares what it takes to move between released versions of DockVault, and each version's support lifecycle. Every release must appear here before it can be cut; the release workflow refuses otherwise. Edges are declared between adjacent releases -- the next release of a line, or the first release of the next line -- and a longer upgrade is composed by walking them. An edge may skip releases only where a release of an older line needs its own way up (for example into the release that carries the same fix on the newer line); it is then at least as cautious as the route it replaces: it requires a backup and is irreversible if any step of that route is, carries every step's conditions, and never passes a release marked `must_land_here`. Every release that is not end-of-life reaches the newest by edges that are not blocked, and no edge leads into a release affected by a vulnerability the release it leaves had fixed. Each version also carries a `support` block: `eol` (end-of-life) and `secure` (free of known unpatched vulnerabilities) are always stated, and an EOL version may carry `code_support` / `security_support` end dates for extended support. The optional top-level `lines` map gives each release line from 0.33 on the day its security fixes end (`security_fixes_until`), null for the newest line, whose end is set when the next minor release ships; it is at least six months after that release. `eol` is the upgrade floor, not the end of security support. The host tool hides EOL releases and refuses to upgrade into or downgrade out of them; a downgrade is refused across any edge marked irreversible. Each known vulnerability is recorded once, in the top-level `advisories`: title, description, impact, remediation, an optional mitigation, a CVSS v4.0 base vector (`cvss`) with the severity band it scores to, an optional id, the `fixed_in` release and the `published` date; `cvss` and `severity` are both null for an unrated advisory. Each affected version lists references to its advisories under `vulnerabilities` (`advisory`, with the advisory's `title` and `fixed_in` repeated for readers that predate advisories; below 0.27.0 a reference carries the advisory id alone). A version affected by any advisory, of any severity, is not secure. An advisory is normally listed only once a release fixes it; one with no fix yet (`fixed_in` null) is published only together with a mitigation.

kinds.direct: The upgrade can be taken in one step. Any caveats are listed in the edge's conditions.
kinds.blocked: The upgrade must not be taken. The edge says why, and what to do instead.

sign-in-fails-without-session-cache.title: Sign-in and credential minting failed or consumed a credential when the session cache was unavailable
sign-in-fails-without-session-cache.description: With the cache down, minting failed while leaving an orphaned credential counting against the caps, a correct-password sign-in failed, and a valid single-use SFTP credential could be refused and consumed.
sign-in-fails-without-session-cache.impact: While the session cache was unreachable, users with the correct password could not sign in, a failed mint left behind a credential that still counted against the account's limits, and a valid single-use SFTP credential could be spent without being used.
sign-in-fails-without-session-cache.remediation: Upgrade to 0.29.1 or later, and revoke any credential a failed mint left behind.

temp-credential-device-management.title: Temporary-credential sessions could manage devices
temp-credential-device-management.description: A temporary credential's web session could enroll a device, grant it vaults the credential was not scoped to, and mint sync credentials, obtaining lasting sync access that outlived the credential.
temp-credential-device-management.impact: A temporary credential, meant to be limited in scope and time, could be turned into lasting sync access -- including to vaults it was never granted -- that survived its expiry and revocation.
temp-credential-device-management.remediation: Upgrade to 0.29.1 or later, then review each account's enrolled devices and revoke any that were enrolled from a temporary credential's session.

device-sync-shares-sign-in-throttle.title: Device sync sign-in attempts shared the interactive sign-in throttle
device-sync-shares-sign-in-throttle.description: Device-sync authentication was throttled in the same per-address bucket as interactive sign-in, so a looping sync client could lock the account's owner out of the web sign-in from the same address; device sync now throttles per device in its own bucket.
device-sync-shares-sign-in-throttle.impact: A sync client that kept failing to authenticate, whether misconfigured or deliberate, could lock every user behind the same address out of web sign-in until the throttle window passed.

note-link-token-stored-in-cleartext.title: Note-link URL tokens were stored in cleartext
note-link-token-stored-in-cleartext.description: A published note link's URL token was stored as given in the database, so anyone who obtained a copy of the database held working links to every live note link; the token is now stored only as a hash and the link keeps working unchanged.
note-link-token-stored-in-cleartext.impact: Anyone holding a copy of the database, such as a leaked backup, held a working link to every published note and could read those notes through the running vault.
note-link-token-stored-in-cleartext.remediation: Upgrade to 0.30.0 or later. Upgrading keeps existing links working, so a link copied out of an older database still opens its note: if a copy of the database may have been exposed, remove those note links and create new ones.

temp-credential-liveness-at-sign-in.title: A temporary credential in use was distinguishable at sign-in
temp-credential-liveness-at-sign-in.description: Signing in with a temporary credential that already had a live session returned a server error while an unusable one returned the ordinary refusal, so the difference told a holder of a guessed name whether that credential was live; both now return the same refusal and count the same against the sign-in throttle.
temp-credential-liveness-at-sign-in.impact: Someone who guessed a temporary credential's name could tell, without its secret, whether that credential was currently signed in, and so aim a guessing attack at live credentials. No secret or data was exposed.

sftp-interrupted-upload-committed.title: An interrupted SFTP upload was committed as a complete file
sftp-interrupted-upload-committed.description: An SFTP upload whose connection dropped before the client closed the file was finalized as though it had completed: nothing distinguished a dropped connection from a graceful close. A partial transfer was stored as a whole file and could replace an existing file of the same name. An upload the client never closed is now discarded instead of committed.
sftp-interrupted-upload-committed.impact: A file could be silently replaced by a truncated copy of an upload that was cut off, and the file's previous content was lost. Anyone able to interrupt a user's connection during an upload could cause it.
sftp-interrupted-upload-committed.remediation: Upgrade to 0.31.0. Files uploaded over SFTP by a connection that dropped part-way may be incomplete; check them against their source.
sftp-interrupted-upload-committed.mitigation: Until you can upgrade, have the SFTP client upload to a temporary name and rename the file into place once the transfer completes (many clients offer this), so an interrupted transfer leaves a partial temporary file instead of replacing the existing one.

sftp-stalled-upload-holds-connection.title: A stalled SFTP upload held its connection indefinitely
sftp-stalled-upload-holds-connection.description: An authenticated SFTP session whose upload stopped making progress kept its worker thread and its connection for as long as the client stayed connected: nothing bounded a session that had signed in and then stopped sending. From 0.19.1, which caps live SFTP connections, enough stalled sessions filled that cap and the server refused every new SFTP connection; before it, each one held a thread with no limit at all. A stalled upload is now failed once it stops making progress, which frees its thread, its connection and the name it was writing.
sftp-stalled-upload-holds-connection.impact: Any user who can sign in over SFTP could stop the SFTP server accepting connections by leaving uploads stalled, for as long as they kept those sessions open. Clients on unreliable connections could do the same by accident.
sftp-stalled-upload-holds-connection.mitigation: Until you can upgrade: on 0.19.1 or later, keep SFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_IP well below SFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS (the defaults, 10 and 100, already are) so that one address cannot hold the whole limit; on any version, restarting the service releases sessions that have stalled.

link-tokens-written-to-access-log.title: Public link tokens were written to the access log
link-tokens-written-to-access-log.description: The token in a note link, public file link or upload link address rides the request path, and the web access log wrote it in full: the access-log filter masked only invitation, share and password-reset addresses. The default container prints that log to docker logs and to the log file the web log pull serves. Rate-limit keys in Redis also held the raw token. A vault password an API client sent in the legacy vault_password query parameter was written to the same log.
link-tokens-written-to-access-log.impact: Anyone who could read the web access log, through docker logs, a copy of the log file, or a web log-pull token an administrator issued, could open a live note link, download through a live file link, or upload into a live upload link, and read any vault password an API client had passed in the query string.
link-tokens-written-to-access-log.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.3. Lines written before the upgrade still hold tokens in docker logs and in any copy of the log file; the web log pull masks them from 0.32.3 on. If someone who should not have those links may have read the logs, revoke and replace the affected links.
link-tokens-written-to-access-log.mitigation: Until you can upgrade, keep the web log pull off (the default) or disable its tokens, and limit who can read docker logs and the vault's log volume.

sign-in-throttle-address-and-name-share-.title: A username could use up an address's sign-in attempts
sign-in-throttle-address-and-name-share-.description: Sign-in attempts are limited per name and per client address, and the two limits were kept under the same kind of key: one for the text typed as the username and one for the address. A sign-in with an address typed as the username was therefore counted against that address. This applies to web and SFTP password sign-in on a default install; the database fallback used while Redis is down already kept them apart.
sign-in-throttle-address-and-name-share-.impact: Anyone, without an account, who knew a client's address could use up half of that address's sign-in attempts within the limit window, slowing down or blocking sign-in for everyone behind that address. No account or data was exposed.
sign-in-throttle-address-and-name-share-.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.5. The two limits are kept apart.
sign-in-throttle-address-and-name-share-.mitigation: None through settings. Blocking repeated failed sign-ins at a proxy in front of the vault limits it.

client-address-forgeable-behind-proxy.title: The client address could be forged behind some proxies
client-address-forgeable-behind-proxy.description: Three ways, none on a default install. With TRUSTED_PROXIES set and a proxy that adds its own X-Forwarded-For header line instead of appending to the client's, the vault read the first line, which the client wrote. With TRUST_ALL_PROXIES=true, it took the left-most address, which is whatever the client wrote unless the proxy replaces the header. And the web server's own forwarded-header handling was on: a connection from 127.0.0.1 (a proxy in the vault's own network namespace, with host networking, or an install outside Docker) that passed the client's header through set the address from it without checking it was an address.
client-address-forgeable-behind-proxy.impact: A client could make the vault record any address in the audit log, sessions and security alerts, spread its sign-in attempts over invented addresses to avoid the per-address limit (the per-account limit still applied), or use up another address's attempts. No data was exposed.
client-address-forgeable-behind-proxy.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.5. Before upgrading, check your proxy settings. A proxy that connects from 127.0.0.1 is no longer trusted on its own: set TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1, or every client appears as 127.0.0.1 and all share one sign-in limit. With TRUST_ALL_PROXIES=true the vault now takes the address the nearest proxy saw, so behind a chain of proxies list each proxy in TRUSTED_PROXIES instead. uvicorn's own FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS is no longer used; the vault applies a trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto itself.
client-address-forgeable-behind-proxy.mitigation: Until you can upgrade, make the proxy replace the X-Forwarded-For header a client sends rather than keep it.

live-monitor-sent-names-to-every-admin.title: The live activity feed sent file and vault names to every administrator
live-monitor-sent-names-to-every-admin.description: Administrators are not members of every vault, and file names are encrypted at rest, as are Standard vault names from 0.14.0. The Live Monitor feed nevertheless carried the file name of every upload and download in a Standard vault, and from 0.14.0 the vault's name, to every signed-in administrator, including vaults they are not a member of and vaults with a vault password.
live-monitor-sent-names-to-every-admin.impact: An administrator could learn the names of files, and from 0.14.0 the names of vaults, that they had no access to. File contents were not exposed, and zero-knowledge vaults were not affected.
live-monitor-sent-names-to-every-admin.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.5. Another account's activity now reaches a watching administrator with only who, from where, when, the kind of event and the vault's id; a person's own activity is unchanged.
live-monitor-sent-names-to-every-admin.mitigation: None through settings. The feed reaches signed-in administrators only.

file-expiry-not-enforced.title: Files past their expiry were not deleted
file-expiry-not-enforced.description: A vault can be set to delete its files a set time after upload, and an upload link sets such a retention on the files it receives. Each file was given its deadline at upload, but nothing ever removed or hid a file once the deadline passed: expired files stayed listed, downloadable over the web and SFTP, and reachable through shares and public file links.
file-expiry-not-enforced.impact: Files were kept, and stayed readable to everyone with access to them, after the deletion the vault's settings promised. An organisation relying on the setting for a retention rule held data longer than its policy allows.
file-expiry-not-enforced.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.6. An expired file disappears from every path at once and is deleted, stored bytes included, within about a minute, with one audit record per file. Files already past their deadline are deleted soon after 0.32.6 first starts; to review them first, set ENFORCE_FILE_EXPIRY=false before upgrading, which keeps the 0.32.5 behaviour until you set it back. Turning a vault's expiry off now also removes the deadline from its files, and at start-up 0.32.6 removes any deadline left on a file in a vault whose expiry is off.
file-expiry-not-enforced.mitigation: Until you upgrade, delete by hand the files that should have expired.

links-kept-working-after-owner-locked.title: Links kept working after their owner was locked or deactivated
links-kept-working-after-owner-locked.description: Locking or deactivating an account ends its sessions, but its links were not always re-checked. Note links never looked at their owner, so they kept serving the note after an administrator locked or deactivated the owner. Public file links and upload links checked only a lock with an end time, so an administrator's lock, which has none, did not stop them.
links-kept-working-after-owner-locked.impact: After an administrator locked or deactivated an account, for example when someone left, anyone holding one of its links could still read the note or download the files it pointed to, and its upload links kept accepting anonymous uploads into the account's vault within the link's limits.
links-kept-working-after-owner-locked.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.6. Note, file and upload links stop while their owner is deactivated or locked by an administrator, and work again when the account is reactivated or unlocked.
links-kept-working-after-owner-locked.mitigation: Until you upgrade, revoke an account's links by hand when you lock or deactivate it, or turn the link features off.

ending-sessions-missed-older-web-session.title: Ending a user's sessions missed some of them
ending-sessions-missed-older-web-session.description: Web requests do not refresh a session's last-activity time, so a periodic cleanup marks a web session inactive once TEMP_CRED_SESSION_GRACE_MINUTES (65 by default) have passed since sign-in, while its token stays valid until the session lifetime ends. Revoking an account's sessions only looked at sessions still marked active. When the session lifetime (the Session timeout setting, or JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES) was longer than that grace time, ending a user's sessions, changing or resetting their password, and signing out other sessions after setting up a second factor all left older web sessions working. Separately, deactivating a user through two routes of the administration API, POST /api/user-management/users/{id}/toggle-active and PUT /api/user-management/users/{id}, revoked none of their sessions; the web app deactivates through a route that did.
ending-sessions-missed-older-web-session.impact: A stolen web session token that had outlived the grace time kept working after the steps meant to cut it off, until the session lifetime ran out. With the default lifetime of 30 minutes the token expires first. A token held when an administrator deactivated its user through either of those API routes worked again once the account was reactivated. While an account is locked or deactivated its tokens are refused, because every request checks that.
ending-sessions-missed-older-web-session.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.6. Revocation now reaches every session that has not already been revoked, and every way of deactivating a user revokes their sessions.
ending-sessions-missed-older-web-session.mitigation: Until you upgrade, keep the session lifetime shorter than TEMP_CRED_SESSION_GRACE_MINUTES (65 minutes by default), and deactivate users from the web app.

zero-knowledge-key-rotated-by-non-holder.title: An administrator without a zero-knowledge vault's key could rotate it and learn the new key
zero-knowledge-key-rotated-by-non-holder.description: A zero-knowledge vault's key is rotated in the browser of whoever starts the rotation: it creates the new key and wraps it for the remaining members. The server let the vault's owner, any administrator or a manager of the vault start a rotation whether or not they held the vault's key, and a rotation does not have to remove anyone. An administrator who was not a member could therefore rotate the key and keep the new one while members went on working.
zero-knowledge-key-rotated-by-non-holder.impact: Such an administrator learned the key protecting every file uploaded to the vault after the rotation. Reading those files also needed their encrypted contents, which the administrator could get with access to the server's storage or through an account they gave access to the vault. Files uploaded before the rotation were not exposed. Every rotation is recorded in the audit log as zk_vault_rekeyed.
zero-knowledge-key-rotated-by-non-holder.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.6. Only an account that holds the vault's current key can rotate it, share it or create its name-index key, and the account that rotates must stay a member. An administrator who removes a member without holding the key removes their access, and the vault then asks its key holders to rotate the key.
zero-knowledge-key-rotated-by-non-holder.mitigation: None through settings. Check the audit log for zk_vault_rekeyed entries by someone who is not a member of that vault.

manager-could-lock-owner-out-of-zero-kno.title: A vault manager could lock the owner out of their own zero-knowledge vault
manager-could-lock-owner-out-of-zero-kno.description: Removing a person from a vault through its permissions switched off that person's zero-knowledge keys before checking that there was a membership to remove. A vault's owner has no membership row, so a request to remove the owner answered that the user had no access to the vault, but had already switched off every key the owner held for it, for every key generation.
manager-could-lock-owner-out-of-zero-kno.impact: A manager of a zero-knowledge vault, or an administrator, could make the vault unreadable to its owner: the owner could no longer open its files or share it, and nothing in the product gave their keys back. Other members kept their access. If the owner was the only one holding the key, nobody could read the vault until an operator switched the owner's keys back on in the database. No content was exposed.
manager-could-lock-owner-out-of-zero-kno.remediation: Upgrade to 0.32.6. The owner cannot be removed through the vault's permissions, and a removal changes nothing unless it removes a membership. The upgrade does not restore an owner who was already locked out: their keys are kept in the vault_member_keys table, marked inactive, and an operator can mark them active again.
manager-could-lock-owner-out-of-zero-kno.mitigation: Until you upgrade, make only people you trust with the vault's availability its managers.

delegated-user-manager-could-take-an-adm.title: A user given the permission to manage users could take an administrator's account
delegated-user-manager-could-take-an-adm.description: An administrator can give someone who is not an administrator the permission to manage users. From 0.23.0 that permission reached POST /users/{id}/reset-link, which makes a password reset link and returns it to the caller, and neither it nor the route that emails one, POST /users/{id}/send-reset-link (from 0.16.0), checked whose account the link was for. Such a user could therefore make a reset link for an administrator, set the administrator's password with it and sign in as them; using the link also ended all of the administrator's sessions. Every other route that changes someone else's account (a second-factor reset, the email address, role, lock and active state, sessions, deletion, SSH keys and the account's details) already required an administrator. From 0.16.0 to 0.22.0 only the emailed link existed. It went to the administrator's own address, so it reached the user who asked for it only if ALLOWED_HOSTS was not set (dockvault.py setup sets it), where the link's host came from that user's request, and the administrator then opened the link. The permission was not held only by people an administrator gave it to: an account created as an administrator (POST /users, or an administrator's invitation) holds it as a stored permission, and demoting the account did not remove it, so every former administrator created as one kept the permission to manage users. In 0.16.0 to 0.32.6 that was another way for a removed administrator to become one again, besides an administrator invitation they had made (administrator-invitation-outlived-its-maker): make a reset link for a remaining administrator and use it (from 0.23.0 directly, before that only through the emailed link as above). The advisory demoted-administrator-kept-the-permission-to-manage-users covers what else a former administrator could do with it.
delegated-user-manager-could-take-an-adm.impact: A user given the permission to manage users could become an administrator without anyone granting it, by taking over an existing administrator's account. As that administrator they could change the deployment's settings, grant any permission, change any account's role, and make reset links for any other user to sign in as them. If the administrator had a second factor enrolled, the second factor was still asked for at sign-in, so the user could not sign in as them. The administrator was still locked out: their password was changed and their sessions were ended. Second factors are optional by default. Each link is recorded in the audit log as password_reset_link_minted or password_reset_link_sent, with who made it and whose account it was for. A link made for an ordinary user also stayed usable after an administrator made that user an administrator, so it set an administrator's password too.
delegated-user-manager-could-take-an-adm.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. A caller who is not an administrator signed in as themselves (a temporary credential never counts as one) may change only an account whose role is not above their own, and never an administrator's. Both reset-link routes check this before a link is made. A refusal is a 403, recorded in the audit log as account_change_refused_role, and no reset token is created. PATCH /users/{id} and the SSH key routes apply the same check, although today only an administrator can reach another person's account through them. Every route that changes someone else's account either requires an administrator or applies this check. The check is made again when a link is used: a reset link made by someone other than its account's owner is judged, when its form is opened and when the new password is set, as its maker and the account stand at that moment. If the maker no longer exists, was deactivated or locked by an administrator, no longer holds the permission to manage users, or may not change the account as it now is (it has been made an administrator, or its role is now above the maker's), the link is refused exactly as an unknown or expired one, deleted, and recorded as password_reset_link_refused with the reason. Making an account an administrator also deletes the open links for it that a non-administrator made, recorded as password_reset_link_revoked. Changing an account's role now resets its permissions to the new role's defaults in the same change, keeping those another administrator granted it and recording what was removed (permissions_reset_for_role), so a demoted administrator no longer keeps the permission to manage users, and a link they made before the demotion is refused when used. Accounts demoted before the upgrade keep what they hold: python dockvault.py accounts --action user-managers lists every account that is not an administrator and may manage users.
delegated-user-manager-could-take-an-adm.mitigation: Until you upgrade, review the permissions of every account that is not an administrator, including former administrators (an account created as an administrator and later demoted keeps the permission to manage users), and remove the Manage Users permission where it is not wanted: the account's Permissions button on the Users page, or DELETE /permissions/users/{id}/revoke/USER_MANAGE. For a former administrator, revoke View Users as well, which from 0.9.0 removes Manage Users with it. After upgrading, do the same for accounts demoted before the upgrade. Search the audit log for password_reset_link_minted and password_reset_link_sent rows made by someone who was not an administrator when they made them (a former administrator included) and whose target_user_id is an administrator's, or belongs to an account made an administrator while the link was still valid (a reset link lasts at most 60 minutes). If you find one, end that administrator's sessions, set their password yourself, and review what the account did after the link was made. A second factor on every administrator account prevents signing in as them, though not the lockout.

demoted-administrator-kept-the-permissio.title: A demoted administrator kept the permission to manage users
demoted-administrator-kept-the-permissio.description: An account created as an administrator (POST /users with the admin role, or from 0.13.0 an administrator's invitation) is given the administrator's default permissions as stored permissions, among them to view users and to manage users. Changing the account's role (PATCH /users/{id}, PUT /api/user-management/users/{id} or PATCH /api/user-management/users/{id}/role) left them in place, and nothing else removed them, so an administrator made a user or an external user kept both, although nobody had granted them to someone who is not an administrator. With the permission to manage users, POST /users/{id}/send-reset-link (from 0.16.0) emails a password reset link for another account and POST /users/{id}/reset-link (from 0.23.0) returns one to the caller. Before 0.33.0 neither checked whose account the link was for, so a former administrator could make a link for a remaining administrator's account and become an administrator again, or for any other account and sign in as that person. A reset link made while still an administrator also stayed usable after the demotion, as every link did before 0.33.0. The permission to view users showed the deployment's counts of users, locked and inactive accounts, active temporary credentials and sessions (GET /api/user-management/metrics) from 0.6.0. The first administrator, created at the first start from ADMIN_USERNAME, and accounts made administrators by a change of role never held these permissions as stored ones, so demoting them left nothing behind.
demoted-administrator-kept-the-permissio.impact: Demoting an administrator did not remove their power over other people's accounts. From 0.23.0 one request made a reset link for another account, and using it set that account's password, ended its sessions and let the former administrator sign in as its owner, with everything that account could open (not a zero-knowledge vault without its key, and a vault with its own password still asked for it). Used on a remaining administrator's account it gave them an administrator's account again, and locked that administrator out; a second factor enrolled on the account was still asked for at sign-in. From 0.16.0 to 0.22.0 only the emailed link existed: it went to the account's own address, and reached the former administrator only if ALLOWED_HOSTS was not set (dockvault.py setup sets it), where the link's host came from their request, and the owner then opened the link. Each link is recorded in the audit log as password_reset_link_minted or password_reset_link_sent, with who made it and whose account it was for. Every administrator can see such an account's permissions under its Permissions button on the Users page once it is no longer an administrator, but nothing pointed to them.
demoted-administrator-kept-the-permissio.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. Changing an account's role now resets its permissions to the new role's defaults in the same change. A permission another administrator granted the account stays, with what it depends on; the old role's defaults, and a permission the account granted itself, are removed. The change is recorded in the audit log as permissions_reset_for_role, with what was removed and added, and the account's notice of the role change names the permissions removed. A reset link made by an account that no longer holds the permission to manage users is refused when used, exactly as an unknown link, and recorded as password_reset_link_refused. 0.33.0 also refuses a reset link for an administrator's account to anyone who is not one. Upgrading does not change accounts demoted before it, because a permission an administrator granted on purpose cannot always be told from a kept one: after upgrading, list the accounts that are not administrators and may view or manage users with python dockvault.py accounts --action user-managers (a kept permission shows no granter). Where it is not wanted, revoke View Users, which removes Manage Users with it. Where it is wanted, revoke it and then grant it, so that it records who granted it and outlasts a later change of role: granting it again while the account still holds it does nothing.
demoted-administrator-kept-the-permissio.mitigation: Until you upgrade, open the Permissions of every account that is not an administrator on the Users page, above all former administrators, and turn off View Users and Manage Users where you did not grant them. From 0.9.0, revoking View Users (DELETE /permissions/users/{id}/revoke/USER_VIEW) removes Manage Users with it; before 0.9.0, revoke each of them. Do the same each time you demote an administrator. To check the past, look in the audit log for password_reset_link_minted and password_reset_link_sent rows made by an account after it stopped being an administrator; if a link was used, end the affected account's sessions, set its password yourself, and review what it did after the link was made.

administrator-invitation-outlived-its-ma.title: A removed administrator could become an administrator again through an invitation they had made
administrator-invitation-outlived-its-ma.description: From 0.13.0 an administrator can invite someone to create an account with the administrator role (POST /invites takes a role, and the web app offers User, External and Admin). Accepting the invitation (POST /invites/{token}/accept, which needs only the link) creates the account with the invitation's role, and neither it nor the lookup that shows the form (GET /invites/{token}) checked who had made the invitation. Demoting, deactivating, locking or deleting the administrator who made it left their pending invitations open; deleting them kept the invitation and only cleared its maker. So an administrator who expected to lose that role could invite an address and username of their own, and after being removed accept the invitation and be an administrator again, under a new account. The invitation had to be accepted before it expired (24 hours by default; an administrator can set up to 30 days) and while invitations were enabled (on by default from 0.19.3; before that, an administrator had to turn them on).
administrator-invitation-outlived-its-ma.impact: An administrator who was removed could regain full administrator access to the deployment: its settings, every account, roles and permissions, the audit log, and password reset links for any account, and in releases before 0.32.6 access to other people's vaults. Removing an administrator did not end the access they could still claim. The pending invitation was listed under Pending invitations on the Users page (the list does not say who made it) until it was accepted, expired or revoked. Its creation is recorded in the audit log as account_invitation_created, by the administrator who made it, and its acceptance as account_invitation_accepted, with the role. Before 0.33.0 the other administrators were not told when an account became an administrator.
administrator-invitation-outlived-its-ma.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. Demoting, deactivating, locking or deleting an administrator revokes the pending invitations they made that would make someone an administrator, each recorded in the audit log as account_invitation_revoked with the reason. Accepting such an invitation, and the lookup that shows its form, are refused unless the administrator who made it is still an active administrator not locked by an administrator; the refusal answers as for an unknown invitation and is recorded as account_invitation_accept_failed with the reason inviter_not_admin. Invitations for other roles are unchanged. In 0.33.0 every administrator is also told when an account becomes an administrator, including through an invitation.
administrator-invitation-outlived-its-ma.mitigation: Until you upgrade, before you remove an administrator, revoke every pending invitation with the Admin role under Pending invitations on the Users page (DELETE /invites/{id}); the audit log's account_invitation_created rows say who made each one, by its token prefix. To check the past, look for account_invitation_accepted rows with role admin and compare each with when the administrator who made the invitation was demoted, deactivated, locked or deleted, which the audit log also records. Turning invitations off in Settings stops every pending invitation from being accepted while you check.

unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in.title: Anyone could stall or crash the web app with large request bodies
unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in.description: The web app limited a request body only by the length the request declared: a declared Content-Length over 256 MiB was refused (up to 0.10.0, over the maximum file size plus 256 MiB). A body sent in chunks declares no length, and nothing limited it at all. The web framework reads a JSON body whole and parses it on the web app's single event loop before a route checks who is calling, so every route that takes a JSON body, sign-in included, read and parsed a body of any size from anyone. Many small JSON objects are the costliest to parse. Measured on 0.32.6: 10 MB of them held every request to the web app for about 9 seconds and raised its memory by about 500 MiB; 20 MB raised it by about 850 MiB, and with the container's memory capped at 640 MiB the web process was killed. The 422 answer to a rejected body also repeated all of it back, which cost as much memory again and returned whatever had been typed, such as a password entered in the username field. The live socket at /ws/monitor had the same fault: anyone could open it, and it parsed the first message before checking who sent it, while the server accepted messages of up to 16 MiB with per-message compression on, so about 16 KB sent on the wire became a 16 MiB message. Measured in-process, one such message held the event loop for about a second and raised the process's memory by about 400 MiB. Nothing limited how often one address opened such a socket.
unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in.impact: Anyone who can reach the web port could, without an account, make the web app unresponsive to everyone for as long as they kept sending such requests or such socket messages, and could get the web process killed, which ends every transfer in progress. With the shipped 4 GB memory limit, about five 20 MB requests sent in parallel from one address, or one of about 90 MB, would be enough, inside the default sign-in rate limit, which counts requests but not their size. No data was exposed.
unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. Every request body is counted as it arrives, whether or not it declares a length, and refused with 413 as soon as it passes its limit, without the rest being read. Anyone who is not signed in may send at most 64 KiB to any route. A larger limit is given only to a session that is signed in at that moment, checked before the body is read: the session exists and has not been ended, the account is active and not locked by an administrator, and a temporary credential is still valid. That session gets 1 MiB on most routes, 8 MiB for a note or an email template, a few MiB for the image uploads, and, for files sent in one multipart request (POST /vaults/{id}/files), MAX_SINGLE_REQUEST_UPLOAD_MB (64 MiB by default, or the largest file the deployment accepts if that is smaller) plus 1 MiB for the form. A token whose session has ended is refused with 401 before any of its body is read. One chunk of a resumable upload may be 64 MiB, signed in or through an upload link, because those routes check the caller before they read. The live socket takes messages of at most 16 KiB without per-message compression, closes on any message over 4 KiB before parsing it, and limits how often one address may connect (RATE_LIMIT_WS_CONNECT, 120 a minute by default). A 422 now returns each error's type, location and message, never the rejected value.
unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in.mitigation: Until you upgrade, put a reverse proxy in front of the vault that limits request body size, counting chunked bodies too (nginx's client_max_body_size does): 1m by default, 65m on the resumable chunk paths (/vaults/*/uploads/*/chunks/* and /receivers/*/upload-session/*/chunks/*), and your largest direct upload on POST /vaults/*/files if you use it. A per-address request rate limit alone does not help. For the live socket, have the proxy remove the Sec-WebSocket-Extensions request header (nginx: proxy_set_header Sec-WebSocket-Extensions "";) so compression is never negotiated, and limit the request rate to /ws/monitor per address (nginx: limit_req).

second-factor-failure-wrote-unbounded-au.title: A failed second-factor sign-in could write audit rows of any size
second-factor-failure-wrote-unbounded-au.description: When the second step of a sign-in failed, its audit row recorded the second-factor method as the client sent it, only lowercased. The field was free text with no length limit, bounded only by the request body: at most 256 MiB when the request declared its length, and not at all when it was sent in chunks (unbounded-request-bodies-before-sign-in). So whoever reached that step, which takes the correct password of an account with a second factor, wrote a row of that size with each failed attempt.
second-factor-failure-wrote-unbounded-au.impact: Any user who set up a second factor on their own account could grow the audit log by up to hundreds of megabytes per request, within the sign-in limits (ten attempts per five minutes from one address), until the database's disk filled and the whole vault stopped working. Reading the audit log also had to load those rows. No data was exposed.
second-factor-failure-wrote-unbounded-au.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. The row records the method only as one of the known names, or as other. After upgrading, look for second_factor_failed rows with unusually large details and delete them if an attack left any.
second-factor-failure-wrote-unbounded-au.mitigation: Until you upgrade, watch the free space on the database's volume and the size of the audit_logs table.

failed-sign-ins-locked-out-the-account-o.title: Wrong passwords from anyone signed a user out and kept them out
failed-sign-ins-locked-out-the-account-o.description: Five wrong passwords for an account (the default login limit), sent by anyone from any address and counted until the account's next successful sign-in or the end of a lock, locked it for the lockout duration (15 minutes by default), and each further wrong password restarted the lock. This automatic lock was enforced like an administrator's: every request from the account's web sessions was refused with a response that tells the browser to delete the site's stored data, which signs the person out in every browser; the account's SFTP connections, its temporary credentials and their sessions stopped; its desktop devices stopped syncing (from 0.28.0); and, up to 0.32.5, its public file links and upload links stopped working. Separately, the sign-in throttle counted attempts per username across all addresses, so the same failed attempts also refused the owner's own sign-in for the rest of the login window.
failed-sign-ins-locked-out-the-account-o.impact: Anyone who knew or guessed a username, the default admin included, could without an account sign that person out everywhere and keep them from signing in, syncing or using SFTP for as long as they kept sending wrong passwords, a few every quarter of an hour. On a deployment with one administrator that also kept everyone from administering it. No account or data was exposed.
failed-sign-ins-locked-out-the-account-o.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. Wrong passwords now lock new sign-ins only from the address they came from (an IPv6 address counts as its /64). A separate account-wide count refuses new sign-ins from every address once it reaches the login limit times ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_BACKSTOP_MULTIPLIER (4 by default, so 20); it holds about the last 24 hours, losing one failure every 24 hours divided by that number (every 72 minutes by default). Neither lock ends a session already signed in, a device's sync, a temporary credential, an SFTP connection or a link; only an administrator's lock does, and an administrator's unlock clears both. The sign-in throttle counts a username per address. Whoever knows a username can still pause new sign-ins to the account: from the person's own address (a shared office network, for example) with the login limit's worth of wrong passwords, for the lockout duration, and from anywhere with 20 in a day, kept paused with one more about every 72 minutes.
failed-sign-ins-locked-out-the-account-o.mitigation: Until you upgrade, limit repeated failed sign-ins at a proxy in front of the vault, and do not give administrators a guessable username such as admin. A shorter lockout duration shortens each lock but does not prevent the sign-out.

temp-credential-heard-other-credentials-.title: A temporary credential learned when the account's other temporary credentials signed in
temp-credential-heard-other-credentials-.description: Every signed-in web session keeps a live connection to the server (a web socket), which tells an account when one of its temporary credentials signs in. The server chose who hears that notice by the account it belongs to, and a temporary credential's session belongs to the account that created it. So while one temporary credential had the web app open, or a socket opened by hand, it received the same notice whenever another temporary credential of that account signed in on the web: that credential's name, the address it signed in from and the time. Sign-ins over SFTP sent no such notice.
temp-credential-heard-other-credentials-.impact: Someone holding one temporary credential, such as an outside party it was given to, could learn the names of the account's other temporary credentials and the addresses and times at which they were used on the web, which can identify the other parties the account works with. No file, vault, password or credential secret was exposed.
temp-credential-heard-other-credentials-.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. A temporary credential's session receives nothing over the web socket; the account's own sessions still receive the notice.
temp-credential-heard-other-credentials-.mitigation: None through settings. Temporary credentials created from different accounts do not hear each other.

demoted-administrator-kept-the-live-feed.title: An administrator whose role was taken away kept receiving the live activity feed
demoted-administrator-kept-the-live-feed.description: The Live Monitor's feed of the whole deployment's activity reached administrators over the web socket each signed-in session keeps open. Whether a socket belonged to an administrator was decided once, when it opened, and never checked again, and changing someone's role ends none of their sessions. A socket opened while the person was an administrator therefore went on receiving the feed after they were made an ordinary user: every sign-in and sign-out with its username and address, temporary credentials' sign-ins with their names, security alerts, and every upload and download with who made it and the vault's id (before 0.32.5, the file and vault names too).
demoted-administrator-kept-the-live-feed.impact: A former administrator could keep watching the deployment's activity after losing the role, until that socket closed or their sessions were ended. They could not act as an administrator: every request checks the role afresh.
demoted-administrator-kept-the-live-feed.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.0. The deployment-wide feed is gone. The Activity page's signal carries only an event's id and category, and a socket stops receiving it within seconds of its account losing the administrator role.
demoted-administrator-kept-the-live-feed.mitigation: Until you upgrade, end a person's sessions when you take the administrator role away from them.

administrators-locked-out-for-good-with-.title: With a lockout duration of 0, failed sign-ins could lock every administrator out for good
administrators-locked-out-for-good-with-.description: ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MINUTES=0 (set in .env; the default is 15, and the Settings page cannot set 0) makes an automatic lock last until an administrator clears it. Wrong passwords typed for an account's name arm the lock, and anyone who knows the name can type them: before 0.33.0 five in a row from anywhere, from 0.33.0 five from one address, or twenty from all addresses together over about a day. An administrator's own account was locked the same way. So wrong passwords for each administrator's name locked every administrator out, and then nobody could clear any lock: the documented way out needed an administrator who could sign in, and the host tool had no unlock. Sessions already signed in kept working.
administrators-locked-out-for-good-with-.impact: On a deployment that set the lockout duration to 0, anyone who knew the administrators' usernames could stop every administrator from signing in, for good. Administration was lost until someone edited the database. No data was exposed or changed, and other users could still sign in.
administrators-locked-out-for-good-with-.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.1. With a lockout duration of 0 an administrator's automatic lock now has an end: a lock on sign-ins from one address ends after 15 minutes, and a pause on sign-ins from every address once its count has also lost a failure (72 minutes with the default settings). One that 0.33.0 armed before the upgrade is given that end at the administrator's next sign-in, or by the periodic release within five minutes of the start. A lock with no end that an earlier release armed is recorded like one an administrator set, and stays until it is cleared, as other accounts' automatic locks do. The host tool of 0.33.1 or later clears an account's locks from the host, recorded as the host operator's change: python dockvault.py accounts --action unlock once the checkout is updated (git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1; an older tool does not offer it), or docker exec vault python -m app.core.host_operator unlock --username NAME --confirm-username NAME (the container is vault-api in the split layout and the local trial). The mitigation's UPDATE statement clears such a lock in the database too, with any lock an administrator set on purpose. Before the upgrade, look for the line ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MINUTES=0 in .env; python dockvault.py update names it only when the tool itself is 0.33.1 or later.
administrators-locked-out-for-good-with-.mitigation: Set ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MINUTES to a positive number in .env (15 is the default) and recreate the containers. If every administrator is already locked out, clear their locks in the database. On 0.33.0: DELETE FROM sign_in_lockouts WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE role = 'ADMIN'). Before 0.33.0: UPDATE users SET is_locked = false, locked_until = NULL, failed_login_attempts = 0 WHERE role = 'ADMIN' (this also removes a lock an administrator set on purpose).

client-address-forgeable-through-docker-.title: The client address could be forged through the Docker gateway when TRUSTED_PROXIES was a range
client-address-forgeable-through-docker-.description: Docker relays some connections to a published port through the container network's gateway, so the vault sees them coming from the gateway's address: clients that connect over IPv6 (on a Docker network without IPv6, the default), clients on the Docker host itself, and on Docker Desktop every client. .env.example suggested setting TRUSTED_PROXIES to a reverse proxy's network, with the example 172.16.0.0/12, which contains the gateway of every network in Docker's default address pools. With such a range the gateway was a trusted proxy, and any of those clients could send its own X-Forwarded-For header and be recorded under an address of its choosing. The shipped secure compose file publishes the web port on every interface. With TRUSTED_PROXIES empty (the default), or listing only proxies' own addresses, nothing changed.
client-address-forgeable-through-docker-.impact: A client could make the vault record any address in the audit log, sessions and security alerts, spread its sign-in attempts over invented addresses to step round the per-address limits (the account-wide limit still applied), or spend another address's allowance and so pause sign-ins to an account from that address. No data was exposed.
client-address-forgeable-through-docker-.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.1. A range in TRUSTED_PROXIES no longer trusts the container's gateway (its default route, read at start); only the token gateway, or the gateway's exact address, does. A proxy container on the vault's network is trusted by a range as before. A reverse proxy on the Docker host connects from the gateway too: for one, set TRUSTED_PROXIES=gateway and publish the web port on loopback only, with WEB_BIND=127.0.0.1 and the secure compose file of 0.33.1 or later. An install that updates by pulling images keeps its compose files, so edit its web port mapping to 127.0.0.1:<port>:8000 by hand. Until then, such a proxy's clients are all recorded as the gateway and share its sign-in limits: the web process says so when it starts, naming the lines to change. Before the upgrade, compare TRUSTED_PROXIES in .env with the gateway that docker network inspect shows for the vault's network; python dockvault.py update says so too when the tool itself is 0.33.1 or later (update the checkout first: git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1).
client-address-forgeable-through-docker-.mitigation: Until you upgrade, list only your proxies' own addresses in TRUSTED_PROXIES, never a range that contains the Docker network's gateway (docker network inspect <network> shows it). For a reverse proxy on the Docker host, list the gateway's exact address and publish the web port on 127.0.0.1 only, so that no client can reach the port past the proxy.

revoked-permission-came-back-after-a-res.title: A permission an administrator revoked came back when the vault restarted
revoked-permission-came-back-after-a-res.description: An administrator can take away from an account a permission its role has by default: to view or download files, to create vaults, to delete files, to share a vault, to hand out temporary credentials, among others. Every start of the web process granted each account that is not an administrator all of its role's default permissions again, so a revoked default came back at the next restart: an upgrade, a container restart, a host reboot. Nothing recorded it. The audit log holds the revocation and no grant, and the Users page shows the permission as held again.
revoked-permission-came-back-after-a-res.impact: An account went on doing what an administrator had taken away, from the next restart on, and nobody was told: for example viewing and downloading files in the vaults it could open, creating vaults, deleting files in vaults it may write to, sharing its vaults, or giving temporary credentials to other people. It could not gain a permission its role does not have by default, and could not reach a vault or file it had no access to.
revoked-permission-came-back-after-a-res.remediation: Upgrade to 0.33.1. Each default permission now records the revision of the defaults in which it became one, and each account the revision it has been given. A start gives an account only the defaults added after that revision, once, and records each grant in the audit log as permission_default_granted. A revoked default stays revoked, and the first start after the upgrade grants nothing. Permissions that an earlier restart granted back are still held. The host tool of 0.33.1 or later lists each account and permission an administrator revoked that a restart then granted again, with when, from the audit log: python dockvault.py accounts --action regranted-defaults once the checkout is updated (git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1; an older tool does not offer it), or docker exec vault python -m app.core.host_operator regranted-defaults (the container is vault-api in the split layout and the local trial). Revoke them again where they are still not wanted.
revoked-permission-came-back-after-a-res.mitigation: Until you upgrade, check the permissions of the accounts you restricted after every restart, and revoke again what came back (the account's Permissions button on the Users page).

0.10.0.notes: No schema change. Every release up to here shares one physical schema: the set of boot DDL statements is byte-identical across all of them, and the model differs only in comment text.

0.11.0.notes: First release to change the physical schema: adds the vault_storage_grants table and a nullable users.storage_quota_bytes column, applied automatically and idempotently at boot. The additions are unused by 0.10.0, so a rollback is clean; take a backup before upgrading.

0.11.1.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.11.0. Security patch: user-controlled values (the failed-login redis key and the alert resolver) are sanitized before they reach the security-monitor logs (log-injection hardening). A rollback is clean and needs no backup.

0.11.2.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.11.0/0.11.1. Security hardening: closes a temporary-credential mint vault-password oracle (vault membership is now verified before the password proof), audits admin-plane and cross-tenant access denials, bounds client-supplied encrypted-name metadata, orders the user-update authorization check before the existence lookup, and re-checks temporary-credential deactivation on the web path every request. A rollback is clean and needs no backup.

0.12.0.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.11.0/0.11.1/0.11.2. Adds credential lock/unlock/change-passphrase plus start/stop/restart/status lifecycle commands to the dockvault.py host management tool, so an operator can seal the .env secrets file into an encrypted .env.enc while a deployment is off (envelope encryption: a Fernet data key wrapped under a scrypt-derived passphrase key, with a stable recovery key). This is a host-tool change only; the container image is functionally unchanged from 0.11.2. Also hardens the test suite. A rollback is clean and needs no backup.

0.13.0.notes: Account onboarding. Adds two tables (account_invitations, email_change_codes), created automatically and idempotently at boot by create_all; both are additive and unused by 0.12.0, so a rollback is clean -- take a backup before upgrading. Verified live: a 0.12.0 stack upgraded to 0.13.0 over the same volume creates both tables (schema complete) and self-signup works. Features: admin account invitations (mint / list / revoke, plus a public single-use accept link); public self-signup gated by an org policy (email requirement, signup domain allow/deny, login identifier username/email/either); self-service email change with an emailed one-time verification code; a last-admin-email lockout guard; and log-access fixes (web log-pull in the split-container shape plus a settings-tab overflow fix).

0.14.0.notes: Adds six additive tables (email_profiles, email_templates, email_resources for the Email Studio; notifications; notes; email_actions), all created automatically and idempotently at boot by create_all and unused by 0.13.0, so a rollback is clean -- take a backup before upgrading. Features: Email Studio (branded HTML email templates with grouped substitution tokens and automated-email actions that route the verification-code / password-reset / invitation emails through the template mechanism, with a fail-safe that never sends a system security email missing its code or link token); an in-app notification bell plus a reworked three-lane non-admin dashboard (What's waiting for you / Favourites / Most recent); move and copy for files and folders, within a vault and across Standard vaults (re-encrypting content under the destination binding; zero-knowledge cross-vault deferred); personal server-side notes with a snapshot 'send note' to other users; and a rate-limiter split giving per-chunk uploads and polled reads their own generous budgets so large uploads and normal polling are no longer throttled.

0.15.0.notes: Public note links + notes UX. Adds two additive tables (note_link_tags, note_public_links), created automatically and idempotently at boot by create_all and unused by 0.14.0, so a rollback is clean -- take a backup before upgrading. Features: public note links -- a note owner can turn a note into an anonymous, tokenized SNAPSHOT link that anyone holding the link can read without signing in, governed by admin-defined 'note-link tags' that act as a security FLOOR the creator may only tighten (a longer token, an added or stronger PIN/password, a shorter expiry, fewer views), with anonymous redemption rate-limited per link, a per-link lockout after repeated wrong secrets, and fail-closed behaviour. Plus a Notes read modal with a left rail; clickable note tiles with wrapping text and bottom-aligned actions; a Send->Share chooser (send a copy to a member, or create a public link); a 'Shared (by me)' tab; live in-app notification delivery over the activity socket so a sent note appears without a page refresh (the socket now persists app-wide and re-checks session revocation); and admin oversight of every public link (list, revoke, and bulk-revoke). Host tool only: dockvault.py setup on a re-run now honours --image-source build so an operator can run freshly-pulled source instead of re-pulling the pinned release.

0.16.0.notes: Email templates & automation, plus notes-UX fixes. Schema: one additive nullable column, email_templates.default_key (created by create_all on a fresh DB, and by the boot DDL ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS on an existing one), plus a partial-unique index over it -- marks a template as the built-in default for an automated-email action; boot seeds a default template per action and pre-binds each action to its default (idempotent, never overwriting an admin's own template or 'none' choice). Two additive tables: otp_codes (the durable fallback for a generalized one-time-code service -- codes live in Redis first, this table when Redis is down; it supersedes email_change_codes, which is retained but no longer written) and password_reset_tokens (single-use, hashed-at-rest tokens for self-service and admin-triggered password-reset links). All additive and unused by 0.15.0, so a rollback is clean -- take a backup before upgrading. Features: a generalized OTP service backing email verification and password reset; self-service + admin-triggered password reset via emailed links; default email templates seeded with 'Load from default' in the Email Studio; and log redaction of sensitive values. Also folds in notes follow-up fixes: the sidebar no longer collapses when a very long note is present; the public-link creator gains a working Done button and disables 'never expires' under a lifetime-capped tag; the Shared tab refreshes live and can view a link's frozen snapshot; the active Notes tab persists across reload; a My-notes count badge; and a new admin 'maximum note size' setting.

0.16.1.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.16.0. Fix: an automated-email SYSTEM action (password reset / account invite / email change) whose built-in default template existed but was left unbound is now bound to it at boot, so editing that template in the Email Studio applies to the sent email instead of being a silent no-op (the send path reads the bound template; an unbound system action previously fell back to the built-in body). Only SYSTEM actions are self-healed -- their 'none' equals the built-in body the default template already carries, so binding never changes what is sent; OPTIONAL actions keep an admin's explicit 'none', and an admin's own custom binding is never overwritten. A rollback is clean and needs no backup.

0.17.0.notes: Minimum supported release. First version to seal names, descriptions and content checksums at rest. Schema: adds vaults.name_key_version and files.enc_checksum, and makes files.checksum_sha256 nullable (the content checksum is sealed into enc_checksum and decrypted on load), all applied by the boot DDL. An image older than 0.17.0 cannot read a deployment written by it: a vault name/description reads back NULL, a note title reads as an opaque sealed token, and a file download fails closed mid-stream because the integrity verifier finds checksum_sha256 NULL. There is therefore no in-place downgrade off it, and no in-place upgrade into it from 0.16.1 -- reach it by deploying fresh and restoring from a backup (see the blocked edge and the waiver). Every release below it is end-of-life.

0.18.1.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.17.0/0.18.0. Follow-up fixes from an external audit of 0.18.0, none a confidentiality break: two vault handlers (update-info, change-password) that answered an authorization failure with 500 now return 403; the ECC key-topology endpoint (/ecc/vaults/{id}/keys) returns 403 for a vault the caller cannot reach instead of leaking mode/dek_version to a non-member or 404-vs-403 confirming existence; the public note-link redeem endpoint adds the missing per-IP rate-limit bucket (token enumeration was unthrottled); chunked-upload completion returns a named 409 (not a 500) for a session it cannot read, and the 0.17.0->0.18.0 downgrade edge now documents that in-flight uploads do not survive a downgrade; the download Content-Disposition header strips forward slashes as well as backslashes; a NUL byte in an uploaded filename is rejected with 400 instead of surfacing as a 500; and the base-image apk-upgrade reproducibility exception is documented and contract-tested. A rollback to 0.18.0 is clean and needs no backup.

0.18.2.notes: Additive schema fix, no data migration. Adds the foreign key for temporary_credentials.created_by_temp_credential_id (self-referential, ON DELETE SET NULL) that create_all already declares but the boot DDL omitted, so a fresh install and an upgraded one converge to the same physical schema. Deleting a temp credential that had minted others now nulls their created_by_temp_credential_id provenance pointer instead of leaving a dangling id (any pre-existing dangling ids are nulled first, so the constraint add cannot fail on an install that ran the earlier column-only DDL). A rollback to 0.18.1 is clean and needs no backup: the older image simply does not re-add the foreign key and the column is unchanged.

0.18.0.notes: No schema change; same physical schema as 0.17.0. Follow-up hardening and fixes on the 0.17.0 at-rest sealing round. At rest: seals a Standard vault's ACTIVE resumable-upload filename and MIME (they were plaintext in chunked_upload_sessions for the life of the upload; the enc_name/enc_mime/name_bi columns already existed and are simply now used for Standard uploads too, decrypted transparently on read), and stops copying already-sealed item/vault names and note titles into the plaintext notification body (the recipient reaches the live item via the deep link). Host tool (dockvault.py): drops the spent ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env after the admin is bootstrapped (only when the DB bootstrap marker confirms an admin exists; fail-closed otherwise); no longer archives a never-used fresh .env when 'deploy a new set' is chosen on a fresh install, and warns in red when a real .env is archived; and lock/status now surface unsealed plaintext .env.* archives. SFTP: the effective per-file upload limit is min(MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB, the RAM staging tmpfs) -- the shipped .env.example defaults are reconciled to agree, the effective SFTP limit is surfaced in the admin settings, and an over-limit or staging-full upload returns a named error instead of a bare 'Failure'. A rollback to 0.17.0 is clean and needs no backup: no persistent schema or data changed, and only an upload in flight at the moment of a downgrade would be affected.

0.19.0.notes: In-vault file operations & previews. Additive schema: files.modified_by (nullable UUID, FK users.id ON DELETE SET NULL) records who last renamed a file in place; the column AND its foreign key are both added by the boot DDL so a fresh create_all install and an upgraded one match. Adds a safe Markdown/HTML/source preview renderer (server-side nh3 allowlist, CSP-locked empty-sandbox srcdoc iframe), a copyable plaintext SHA-256 (Standard vaults, download-gated), a Move/Copy staging panel, upload fixes, live download progress, and bounded-memory preview (large media refused inline, big text windowed via Range). Depends on Markdown 3.10.3 + Pygments 2.20.0 (hash-pinned, pure-Python). A rollback to 0.18.2 is clean and needs no backup: the modified_by column is left in place and simply ignored by the older image.

0.19.1.notes: No schema change. Security & authorization hardening from the v0.19.0 review: an SFTP pre-auth connection admission (a total + per-source-IP connection ceiling and an auth grace timeout, the SSH MaxStartups equivalent) so a no-credential connection flood can't exhaust threads and Transports; a password change now durably revokes the account's sessions on the self-service and admin paths, matching the reset path; regular web sessions get an absolute server-side expiry so abandoned rows age out, and session_timeout is clamped to a 30-day maximum; new password key-encryption-key wraps derive at 600,000 PBKDF2 iterations (existing wraps still open at their stored count); and denial tests plus a coverage guard for the four destructive vault capabilities. Adds SFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS / SFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_IP / SFTP_AUTH_GRACE_SECONDS settings (defaults suit a single tenant). A rollback to 0.19.0 is clean and needs no backup: no persistent schema or data changed.

0.19.2.notes: No schema change. Follow-up security cleanup from the v0.19.0 security review: the ECC name-index-key GET and the member-keys GET now refuse a non-member with 403 whether or not the vault exists, so neither confirms a vault id to a stranger (parity with the DEK keys endpoint); POST /ecc/keys/register refuses a temporary session before charging the account's ECC register rate budget, so a refused temp request can no longer spend the owner's once-per-account budget; plus regression tests pinning cross-tenant file-plane access at 403-not-500 and the temp-credential scope contract. A rollback to 0.19.1 is clean and needs no backup: no persistent schema or data changed.

0.19.3.notes: No schema change. Collaboration features now default ON for a fresh self-hosted install: internal file sharing, public note links, and admin invite-by-link. These are admin master switches that previously shipped off-by-default; an explicit stored 'off' is still honored, and nothing is exposed until a user actively creates a share or link (invite-by-link is admin-only). Self-signup stays off by default. A rollback to 0.19.2 is clean and needs no backup: no persistent schema or data changed.

0.20.0.notes: Adds optional two-factor authentication. A user can enroll an authenticator app (TOTP) with mandatory recovery codes; login becomes two-step for an enrolled or required account. An admin can require two-factor (forced enrollment at next sign-in), scope step-up per high-risk action (require the authenticator and/or a password re-authentication), and require a temporary credential for SFTP when an account's second factor is in effect. New two-factor tables are created automatically by the app on first start -- no migration step. A rollback to 0.19.3 leaves those tables and their data intact but DISABLES two-factor enforcement (accounts then sign in with their password only) until you upgrade again.

0.21.0.notes: Adds public links for files and folders ("secure send"): an admin can enable anonymous, tokenized links that let anyone with the URL download one file or one folder of a Standard vault, governed by the existing public-link tags (token-length floor, optional PIN/password, expiry, use cap) and revocable at any time. The link token is stored hashed and shown once at creation; the anonymous read path re-checks the owner's access on every request. New public_links table and a note_link_tags.allowed_targets column are created automatically at boot -- no migration step, and no existing data is changed. A rollback to 0.20.0 leaves the table and column intact but stops serving public file links until you upgrade again.

0.22.0.notes: Adds upload links ("receivers"): an admin can enable anonymous, tokenized links that let anyone with the URL upload files into a dedicated, owner-paid Standard vault, governed by receiver tags (token-length floor, optional PIN/password, expiry, per-file and total size caps, retention) and revocable or pausable at any time. The link token is stored hashed and shown once. Anonymous uploads reserve their declared size against the receiver's cap before any bytes move, are admitted on a separate transfer budget so they cannot starve signed-in transfers, and can only ever land in the receiver's own vault. New receivers, receiver_tags and receiver_upload_sessions tables plus a receivers.reserved_bytes column are created automatically at boot -- no migration step, and no existing data is changed. A rollback to 0.21.0 leaves the tables intact but stops serving upload links until you upgrade again.

0.23.0.notes: Adds the owner and admin UI for the public file/folder links ("secure send", backend added in 0.21.0) and upload links ("receivers", 0.22.0), which previously shipped with no interface: create, manage and revoke links, and govern them with tags and per-feature settings. Also a round of two-factor and settings usability fixes -- a full-size enrollment QR code, an MFA column in the accounts list, a single-step-up save for the whole step-up action matrix, an admin "copy reset link" action for accounts with no email, and a reworked rate-limit settings surface that shows each limit's read-only deployment value beside an optional, bounded custom override (now extended to the login, vault-unlock and SFTP throttles). No schema change and no existing data is altered; a rollback to 0.22.0 simply hides the new UI.

0.24.0.notes: Security-hardening release. Adds admin-configurable per-user resource limits (a vault-count cap, a per-account storage budget defaulting to 50 GB, and a cap on active temporary credentials; 0 means unlimited and administrators are exempt), tightens authorization on the file plane (opening an SFTP/chunked upload session now requires write permission, and a nonexistent vault answers 404 instead of 500), hardens a zero-knowledge vault-name re-seal against a future key epoch that would make the name undecryptable, sandboxes the in-browser PDF/media preview, clears the vault list and upload state on logout, keeps the account second-factor requirement from being switched off, bounds the admin login-attempt override, and removes the Server header. No schema change and no existing data is altered; a rollback to 0.23.0 simply restores the prior limits and header behaviour.

0.25.0.notes: Adds a memory-bounded streaming SFTP upload behind a default-OFF flag (SFTP_STREAMING_UPLOAD). When enabled, an SFTP upload encrypts and persists 1 MiB records as they arrive instead of buffering the whole plaintext to the .sftp_tmp staging tmpfs, so RAM/tmpfs use is bounded to one record plus a small reorder window regardless of file size, and the per-file limit is no longer tied to the tmpfs size. The at-rest format is byte-identical to the buffered/web upload path (same codec, 1 MiB records, monotonic AEAD index), so streamed and web-uploaded files are mutually decryptable. All the close-time authorization gates (membership, folder scope, vault password, vault size limit, plan ceiling, and a write-permission re-check) run before the file record commits, and any failure leaves no orphan blob and never destroys an existing same-name file. Adds SFTP_STREAMING_UPLOAD and SFTP_STREAMING_REORDER_MB settings. No schema change; ships OFF, so a rollback to 0.24.0 is clean.

0.26.0.notes: UI polish across the app — no schema change and no new required configuration. Vault cards show a Standard/Zero-knowledge badge; the department access list in a vault's Permissions tab is now the same table as the per-user list with inline level editing, a members modal, and member/granted columns; the audit log paginates and each row opens an 80vw event modal with a table-of-contents of the page's events; the live monitor paginates and a failed login second factor is now recorded and broadcast; the Upload Links page has Links and Drop-vaults tabs (the throwaway drop vaults are also hidden from the main Vaults page); a public file link now counts a use on the actual download rather than on the landing-page visit (a peek returns metadata without consuming a use); native confirm()/alert() dialogs are replaced by the app's themed ones; several tables and the settings tab strip are tightened; and the anonymous share pages get calmer styling. Adds no new environment settings; a rollback to 0.25.0 is clean.

0.27.0.notes: Adds the full SFTP host public key to the host-key endpoint (GET /sftp/host-key) so a client can pin the server's SFTP identity, alongside the existing fingerprint. No schema change, no new required configuration, and no new environment settings; a rollback to 0.26.0 is clean.

0.28.0.notes: Device-scoped SFTP sync credentials. Lets a registered device sync a Standard vault over SFTP without ever holding the vault password: the account proves the vault password once, at grant time, which binds the proof to that device, and the device thereafter holds only a per-device, server-scoped, revocable secret (an opaque token, stored only as its hash) from which the server mints single-use, short-lived SFTP credentials. Additive schema, applied so a fresh install and an upgrade converge: two new tables (devices, device_grants) created by create_all, plus a nullable temporary_credentials.device_id column (FK devices.id ON DELETE SET NULL, tagging a minted credential with the device that minted it) added by the boot DDL ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS. All additions are unused by 0.27.0, so a rollback to 0.27.0 is clean -- it leaves the two tables and the column in place and simply stops serving device credentials until you upgrade again. Adds device-sync settings: a per-account device cap (MAX_DEVICES_PER_USER), a per-device credential cap (MAX_DEVICE_SYNC_CREDS_PER_DEVICE), a previous-secret rotation grace window (DEVICE_SECRET_ROTATION_GRACE_MINUTES), the retired-secret reuse-response posture (DEVICE_SECRET_REUSE_HARD_REVOKE), and an advertised SFTP hostname; the defaults suit a single tenant.
