0.29.0.notes: Eleven product improvements and their fixes. Bugs: the file list is no longer empty after an idle-lock re-login; a vault's hover bar and its menu are now mutually exclusive; opening a vault from Upload links stays on that page and Back returns there. Defaults for NEW vaults and links only: a new vault defaults to 5 GiB (bounded by the account's remaining headroom, and refused below a usable floor exactly as an explicit request would be); a new upload link defaults to a 1 GiB budget. Audit Log: live updates, a compact table view, filters by user and by date-and-time (sent as explicit instants, so they mean the same thing in every time zone), and audit rows for access-control actions that previously wrote none -- group membership and group vault access now record who gained or lost what, and only when something changed. Upload links: the created-link dialog shows the link once with a Done button; the drop-vault card reports its usage and offers Copy link; replacing a link is gated exactly as creating one (step-up, the feature switch and the tag allowlist); 'drop box' is now 'drop vault'. First bootstrap only: temporary vault passcodes, public file and folder links, and upload links start switched on. Starter tags for sharing, public links and upload links are added to any deployment that has none of that kind and has not switched the feature on itself, and the public-link starter tags now say exactly what they permit (the short no-expiry tag publishes notes only; the long-token tags publish notes, files and folders). The 50 GiB account quota (now shown live in Settings), sharing, public note links and invite-by-link were already on by default for every deployment and are unchanged. An existing deployment upgraded to this version keeps every setting and every tag it had. Groups: 'Load from template' presets with an editable tree. Signing out clears every link shown during the session. No schema change: the only model edit is the Python-side default for a new vault's size, so an upgrade alters no existing row and a rollback to 0.28.0 is clean.

0.29.1.notes: Security fix; every deployment on 0.28.0 or 0.29.0 should upgrade. A temporary credential's web session could manage the owner's devices -- enroll a device that never expires, grant it vaults the credential itself was not scoped to, and so obtain lasting sync access that outlived the credential; the device routes now refuse temporary sessions. Signing in and minting a credential no longer fail, leave an orphaned credential counting against the caps, or spend a valid single-use credential when the session cache is unavailable. A device's sync credential is refused at the web sign-in, where it has no legitimate use. No schema change; a rollback to 0.29.0 is clean but reopens the fixed behaviour.

0.30.0.notes: Device sync is throttled per device in its own bucket, so a looping sync client can no longer lock the owner out of the web sign-in from the same address; a device can ask the server whether it may sync before it tries; a sync credential frees its slot when its connection closes; an in-progress SFTP upload shows in the web listing, and while it runs a second upload of its name is refused, from the web page as well as over SFTP (from 0.32.0 every upload holds its name the same way -- web page, API and SFTP alike -- in Standard vaults); note-link URL tokens are stored hashed with an in-place migration and links can be shown again only by their owner through an encrypted copy; SFTP uploads stream to storage by default within a documented memory ceiling, browser downloads stream to disk by default, and a file too large to hold in memory is refused up front instead of buffered when streaming is unavailable; the version lifecycle shown by the app and the host tool comes from the current matrix, not the release's frozen copy; database waits are bounded; the host tool's update no longer changes the deployment's image reference until the new image has actually been pulled. 0.31.0.notes: An SFTP upload that stops making progress is failed instead of holding its thread, its connection slot and the lock on its filename until the client chooses to leave, and an upload the client never closed is discarded rather than committed as a complete file; in the split profile, the SFTP container's healthcheck reports whether the SFTP server is still working rather than whether its port is bound (the combined profile's health check still only tests that the port accepts connections); an abandoned upload's name is freed in five minutes instead of fifteen. A web upload is aborted at sign-out, so an upload in flight cannot outlive the session that started it; a re-picked file is checked against what the server already holds before an interrupted upload continues with it, so an edited file is never spliced onto the previous attempt's chunks; and every upload is told about an earlier upload of its name that is still in progress. No database connection is held while a client sends an upload chunk, and a chunk's whole authorisation is re-established after its body rather than only before it. Every Retry-After is computed in one place -- never below a second, never above its window, and never negative. Where an upload refusal names the member holding the name, it does so only to a viewer shown to be a member. The SFTP per-address limit is split so a device fleet behind one address is not turned away by the flood guard, while the guard against unauthenticated floods is unchanged. A hung Redis breaker probe is replaced instead of a request probing in the foreground. Plain HTTP to a loopback host is treated as a secure context by the browsers' own rule, so a vault served at a .localhost name streams downloads instead of buffering them. Zero-knowledge vaults now write the version-2 key-wrap and content formats, which 0.30.0 already reads, so a rollback to 0.30.0 still opens everything written after the switch; because this is the first release to write them, the upgrade asks for a backup first. The upgrade matrix records each known vulnerability once, with its impact, what to do about it and a CVSS v4.0 rating, and `dockvault.py update` shows each release's known vulnerabilities by severity, says what a change fixes or brings back, and names a release with fewer when there is one. A rollback to 0.30.0 is clean: this release changes no database table, and the one column it writes is read by nothing.

0.32.0.notes: An upload now holds its file name while it runs, whichever way it arrives -- from the web page, through the API or over SFTP -- so a second upload of that name by another route or another member is refused instead of replacing the first when it lands, and another member's web upload shows in the listing as an upload in progress (Standard vaults; a zero-knowledge vault's names never reach the server). In the combined profile /health reads the SFTP server's heartbeat -- "unresponsive" once it stops, "unreachable" if it never started, both reported as degraded -- and the container's healthcheck fails when its SFTP half is down, so a hung SFTP server marks the container unhealthy five to six minutes after the stall at the defaults. The web healthcheck is now the image's own in every compose file, so it always matches the image that runs; a deployment updated by pulling the image, whose secure compose file still names the older check, keeps that check, which does not cover SFTP, until the file is updated. BRAND_ENABLE_SIGNUP=false now rules self-signup out for the whole deployment whatever the admin's switch says; the default, true, leaves the admin's switch in charge. A vault created without a size holds 10 GB instead of 5, the same as the largest single file a fresh install accepts, though the web page's Create vault dialog still filled in 5 GB, so a vault made there held 5 GB unless the number was changed (fixed in 0.32.1); existing vaults keep their size, and under the default 50 GB account budget a regular user fits five default-size vaults instead of ten. Settings accepts a session length of up to 30 days, as the server already did. `dockvault.py update` says a backup is required, and why, whenever it will ask for one. .env.example no longer sets MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB=512, which capped any install that copied it at 512 MB: if your .env still has that line, remove it to get the 10 GB default. LOG_FILE_PATH is retired; nothing wrote it, and an .env that still sets it keeps working. Help text, setting descriptions and the 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 notes now say what the code does. A release candidate's tests now include the Windows and Ubuntu fast lanes, and the setup test requires the previous release's image to turn healthy under the new compose files. No schema change; a rollback to 0.31.1 is clean, except that self-signup goes back to the admin's switch alone, and a name being uploaded from the web page at that moment stays locked for up to five minutes.

0.32.6.notes: Security fixes, five advisories. Files past their expiry are hidden at once and deleted within about a minute, with an audit record per file; turning a vault's expiry off removes its files' deadlines, and an expiry longer than 100 years is refused. Links stop while their owner is deactivated or locked by an administrator; a lock armed by wrong passwords no longer pauses them. Ending a user's sessions, changing or resetting a password, and signing out other sessions after setting up a second factor now also reach web sessions that went idle, and every way of deactivating a user now ends their sessions. Only an account that holds a zero-knowledge vault's current key can rotate it, share it or create its name-index key; a member removed by someone without the key stays removed, and the vault asks its key holders to rotate. A vault's owner can no longer be removed through the vault's permissions, which could switch off the owner's zero-knowledge keys. Administrators can no longer give themselves access to another person's vault or to a file shared with a department, cannot demote, deactivate or lock their own account, and the last active administrator cannot be removed. An SFTP sign-in is refused when its policy check fails. Automatic account locks and unlocks are audited, and finished session and sign-in rows are deleted after 30 days. Before upgrading: files already past their deadline are deleted soon after 0.32.6 first starts, so set ENFORCE_FILE_EXPIRY=false to review them first (a vault whose expiry is off keeps its files). With a single administrator, only a vault's owner can now give that administrator access to the vault. No schema change; a rollback to 0.32.5 is clean, but files deleted by expiry stay deleted.

0.33.0.notes: Security fixes, eight advisories, and the Activity page. A change of role now resets the account's permissions to the new role's defaults, keeping those another administrator granted it, so a demoted administrator no longer keeps the permissions to view and manage users; accounts demoted before 0.33.0 keep them until reviewed (the upgrade condition review-former-administrators; python dockvault.py accounts --action user-managers lists every account that may view or manage users without being an administrator). A user given the permission to manage users can no longer make a reset link for an administrator or for anyone whose role is above theirs (403), and a second change of theirs to someone's sign-in details within 14 days is refused (409). A reset link someone else made is judged again when it is used, and refused as an unknown link once its maker could no longer make it; making an account an administrator revokes the open links a non-administrator made for it. Demoting, deactivating, locking or deleting an administrator revokes the invitations they made to be an administrator, and such an invitation is accepted only while its maker is still an active administrator. Wrong passwords lock new sign-ins only from the address they came from, with a count per account over about 24 hours from all addresses, and an automatic lock no longer signs anyone out or stops their devices, temporary credentials, SFTP connections or links. Request bodies are counted as they arrive and refused with 413 past their route's limit (64 KiB before sign-in, 1 MiB for most routes when signed in), the live socket bounds its messages and its connections per address (RATE_LIMIT_WS_CONNECT), and a 422 no longer repeats the rejected input. A failed second-factor sign-in records its method only by a known name. A temporary credential no longer hears the account's other temporary credentials sign in, and the live signal stops within seconds for an account that loses the administrator role. The Activity page replaces the Live Monitor and Settings, Audit Log: a summary band whose charts filter, a live list of every audited event with its detail beside it, numbered pages or loading as you scroll, saved searches and an export. Every change is now audited, with the way it came in, its route and its user agent. A second change to another person's sign-in details within 14 days needs the approval of another administrator independent of it, the server's operator can reset an account or approve a held change from the host with python dockvault.py accounts, users are told of every administrator's change to their account, and every other administrator is told when an account becomes an administrator. An upload link's owner can change how long it keeps uploads. A folder delete that cannot delete all its files keeps the folder; before, a file moved in during the delete could be lost with its bytes left on disk and the vault counted fuller than it was. Hide note text is kept on the account. For scripts: GET /monitor/stats and GET /audit/export are gone; export the audit log with GET /activity/export (CSV or NDJSON, up to 100,000 rows per export, each export audited), and GET /audit/log is unchanged. Files sent in one multipart request to POST /vaults/{id}/files are capped at 64 MiB (MAX_SINGLE_REQUEST_UPLOAD_MB, never more than the largest file allowed; 0 turns the cap off) and a larger request is answered 413: send large files through the resumable upload, as the web app, the desktop app and the upload-link page already do. A JSON body over 1 MiB is refused with 413 (8 MiB for a note or an email template). Personal data this release stores (docs/data-inventory.md lists every store): audit rows now also carry the browser's user agent (up to 512 characters), the HTTP method, the route and the channel, also for people with no account who open a public link or send through an upload link, and a temporary credential's name after the credential is deleted, to say who did what and how, kept as long as the audit log (for ever with the default AUDIT_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS=0). Names typed at failed sign-ins, which can be a password typed as a username, were already audited; the Activity page lists them and its export includes them. sign_in_lockouts holds failed sign-ins per account and source address and per account over about 24 hours, for the automatic locks: a count goes about a day after its last failure, a lock when it ends. credential_changes holds the requesting and deciding administrators, a summary that can hold a new email address or an SSH key's name and fingerprint, and for an email change the address before and after, for the approval rule and for the 14 days a reset the person asks for goes to the address before; while a request waits it also holds what the change would set (a password hash, an address or a key) and the ids of the administrators the approval rule weighs, cleared when the request is decided or expires (at most 7 days); each record goes 14 days after the change or decision. users.second_factor_reset_at records when an administrator reset the person's second factor, so that their next sign-in sets it up again, and is cleared once they have. admin_grants holds who made each administrator one and when, for the approval rule, while the account is an administrator; an administrator's invitation keeps the administrators its maker descends from, with the invitation. activity_saved_searches holds up to 50 saved filters per administrator, which can hold usernames and addresses, until deleted. The notices and the emails Account changed by an administrator and New administrator name the administrator and, for an email change, both addresses (the email masks the new one); a notice stays until the person deletes it. An Activity export holds usernames, addresses and user agents wherever it is saved. Hide note text and the Activity page's choices are kept on the account. The cache keys and the fallback table that count failed sign-ins by name now hold a keyed stand-in, not the name as typed. The Live Monitor's feed to every administrator's open page is gone. Schema: new tables activity_saved_searches, admin_grants, credential_changes and sign_in_lockouts, and nullable columns audit_logs.channel, audit_logs.temp_credential_name, users.second_factor_reset_at, account_invitations.inviter_lineage and password_reset_tokens.made_by_other, created at the first start. A rollback to 0.32.6 works, since it ignores all of them, but brings back 0.32.6's flaws: among them, an account made an administrator on 0.33.0 holds the administrator's permissions as stored rows, and a demotion on 0.32.6 leaves them in place, so after rolling forward again review the accounts the review-former-administrators check lists. Requests waiting for approval are not applied, automatic locks made by 0.33.0 are forgotten while an account with five or more failed sign-ins since its last successful one is locked at its next wrong password, a second-factor reset no longer asks the user to set the factor up again, and Hide note text is off until chosen again. 0.33.x receives security fixes until six months after 0.34.0 ships (.github/SECURITY.md).

0.33.1.notes: Security fixes, three advisories, and the release tooling for supporting two release lines. python dockvault.py update runs the host tool already installed, and the checks and host actions named below are in the tool of 0.33.1, so update the checkout first (git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1): an older tool checks none of them and offers neither action. A range in TRUSTED_PROXIES no longer trusts the Docker network's gateway, which every connection Docker relays to a published port comes from (IPv6 clients, clients on the Docker host, on Docker Desktop every client), so those clients can no longer set their own address; only the token gateway or the gateway's exact address trusts it. A reverse proxy on the Docker host arrives from the gateway too: for one, set TRUSTED_PROXIES=gateway and publish the web port on loopback only (WEB_BIND=127.0.0.1 with the secure compose file of 0.33.1; an install that updates by pulling images keeps its compose files and edits its port mapping to 127.0.0.1:<port>:8000 by hand). Until then all of such a proxy's clients are recorded as the gateway and share one set of sign-in limits; the web process says so at start, and the update of 0.33.1's host tool says so before the upgrade (the upgrade condition gateway-no-longer-covered-by-ranges, which says how to check by hand). A permission an administrator revoked from an account now stays revoked when the vault restarts: a start gives an account only the role defaults added in a later release, once, each audited as permission_default_granted. Permissions an earlier restart gave back are still held: after the upgrade, 0.33.1's python dockvault.py accounts --action regranted-defaults lists them (the upgrade condition role-defaults-granted-once). With ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MINUTES=0 an administrator's automatic lock now has an end (15 minutes; a pause from every address once its count has lost a failure, 72 minutes by default), one that 0.33.0 armed and is already in place included, while other accounts' automatic locks still last until cleared, and so does a lock with no end from a release before 0.33.0, which is recorded like one an administrator set; with that setting, locking a name shows whether it is an administrator's, because its lock ends. 0.33.1's python dockvault.py accounts --action unlock clears an account's locks from the host, audited as the host operator. A right password no longer counts against the sign-in throttle, so one person signing in again and again, or many accounts behind one address, are no longer refused; wrong passwords count as before, and more right-password sign-ins at the same moment from one address than the login limit (5 by default) still have their extras refused. A password sign-in over SFTP no longer ends the account's other SFTP connections, and a web sign-in no longer ends SFTP connections, which also dropped an SSH-key upload in flight; ending an account's sessions, locking or deactivating it still ends all of them. The database session now runs in UTC whatever the database server's time zone, so times the database stamps are no longer off by that zone's offset. From this release on, the web and SFTP processes read data_requirements before they touch the database and refuse to start when a newer release has marked the data as needing a newer version, naming what changed and how to undo it with that release; ALLOW_START_ON_NEWER_DATA=true starts them anyway. No release writes such a mark yet, and 0.33.0 and earlier do not read it, so a rollback to them is not protected by it. Release lines: each release is published as :vX.Y.Z, the newest release of each line also as :vX.Y (for example :v0.33), and :latest and GitHub's latest release name only the highest version, so a patch release of an older line never moves them; a release tag must be an annotated tag. The upgrade matrix states until when each release line gets security fixes, and lists an advisory by its id alone on versions below 0.27.0. python dockvault.py update and the in-app update check show the newest release of the install's line and until when the line gets security fixes, and an install on an older line is shown a banner when a newer release of its line exists or its line's security fixes have ended; to know about older lines without telling GitHub which one the install runs, the update check, when it is on, also fetches the published matrix of the newest release of each older line the matrix lists (at most five). The image scan fails when a reviewed VEX statement names a package version the image no longer contains; the stale OpenSSL statement was removed. The image sets FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS empty. The JWT library PyJWT is updated from 2.13.0 to 2.15.1, which fixes eleven advisories in it. One of them reached the vault: a bearer token whose header was nested deeper than the stack made a signed-in route answer 500 instead of 401 (GHSA-8wjv-2p76-3863). That exposed nothing and skipped no check, so the vault has no advisory for it; such a token is now refused with 401 like any other invalid one. A bearer token longer than 8,192 characters, far longer than any the vault signs, is now refused the same way without being decoded, so a very long token no longer costs the server time to reject. Accepted residual, published in .github/SECURITY.md: an administrator whose current password someone else set can still approve another administrator's credential change, so whoever set that password can approve through that account; 0.34.0 refuses such approvals. Personal data this release stores (docs/data-inventory.md lists every store): active_sessions.channel records whether a session was signed in over the web or SFTP, and users.permission_defaults_revision the revision of its role's defaults an account has been given; the audit log records each permission a start grants (permission_default_granted) and each unlock from the host. The host tool can list the permissions an administrator revoked that a restart before 0.33.1 granted again, with usernames, roles and times read from the audit log, on the host's terminal and not audited. data_requirements holds no personal data. Schema: new table data_requirements and nullable columns users.permission_defaults_revision and active_sessions.channel, created at the first start. A rollback to 0.33.0 works, since it ignores all of them, but brings back 0.33.0's flaws: its first start grants revoked defaults again, an administrator's lock can last for good again, a range trusts the gateway again, sign-ins end other channels' sessions again, and it does not read data_requirements. 0.33.x receives security fixes until six months after 0.34.0 ships (.github/SECURITY.md).

conditions.summary: A deployment written by 0.17.0 seals names, descriptions and checksums at rest; an image older than 0.17.0 reads them as NULL or an opaque token and fails a file download closed mid-stream. The presence of files.enc_checksum is the durable signal that this data cannot be served by an older image.

conditions.summary: Stored data is unaffected by a downgrade to 0.17.0 (vault names, descriptions, notes and files all still read correctly). The one exception is a resumable upload that is IN FLIGHT across the downgrade: 0.18.0 seals the active session's filename and 0.17.0 has no decrypt event for it, so that unfinished transfer cannot be completed on 0.17.0 (the file is not lost - only that in-progress upload). Complete or cancel in-progress uploads before downgrading.
conditions.detect: SELECT 1 FROM chunked_upload_sessions WHERE status='active' AND filename IS NULL AND enc_name IS NOT NULL

conditions.summary: 0.32.6 enforces file expiry, which no earlier release did: within about a minute of its first start it deletes every file whose deadline has passed in a vault whose expiry is on, stored bytes included, and that cannot be undone by rolling back. To review those files first, set ENFORCE_FILE_EXPIRY=false before upgrading, and set it back when you are done; turning a vault's expiry off keeps its files.
conditions.detect: SELECT count(*) FROM files f JOIN vaults v ON v.id = f.vault_id WHERE f.expires_at IS NOT NULL AND f.expires_at < (now() AT TIME ZONE 'utc') AND v.expire_files_after_days > 0

conditions.summary: Before 0.33.0, an administrator made a user or an external user kept the permissions to manage and to view users that an account created as an administrator holds, though nobody had granted them to a non-administrator. With them the account could still make password reset links for other people's accounts, and in 0.16.0 to 0.32.6 for an administrator's, and so become an administrator again. From 0.33.0 a change of role resets an account's permissions to the new role's defaults, but accounts demoted before the upgrade keep what they hold, because a permission an administrator granted on purpose cannot always be told apart. After upgrading, review every account that is not an administrator and holds Manage Users or View Users, above all former administrators. 'python dockvault.py accounts --action user-managers' lists them, as does the check below; '(no granter recorded)' marks a permission kept from an administrator account, or one whose granter was deleted. Where it is not wanted, revoke View Users under the account's Permissions button on the Users page, which removes Manage Users with it; revoking only Manage Users leaves View Users. Where it is wanted, revoke it and then grant it, so that it records who granted it and outlasts a later change of role: granting it again while the account still holds it does nothing.
conditions.detect: SELECT u.username, u.role, u.is_active AS active, p.endpoint_group AS permission, coalesce(g.username, '(no granter recorded)') AS granted_by, p.granted_at FROM user_endpoint_permissions p JOIN users u ON u.id = p.user_id LEFT JOIN users g ON g.id = p.granted_by WHERE u.role <> 'ADMIN' AND p.endpoint_group IN ('USER_MANAGE', 'USER_VIEW') ORDER BY (p.granted_by IS NULL) DESC, u.username, p.endpoint_group

conditions.summary: The Activity page replaces the Live Monitor page and the Audit Log tab in Settings. GET /monitor/stats and GET /audit/export are removed: a script that exports the audit log must move to GET /activity/export (CSV or NDJSON, up to 100,000 rows per export, and each export is itself audited). GET /audit/log is unchanged.

Wrong passwords now lock new sign-ins to an account only from the address they came from (an IPv6 address counts as its /64), after the login limit (5 by default). A count per account from all addresses together, over about 24 hours, pauses new sign-ins from every address once it reaches the login limit times ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_BACKSTOP_MULTIPLIER (4 by default, so 20), and it loses one failure every 24 hours divided by that number (every 72 minutes by default): so no more than about 20 passwords a day are checked for an account, where 0.32.6's sign-in throttle let 5 through every 5 minutes, and whoever knows a username can keep new sign-ins to it paused for everyone, its owner included, with one more wrong password about every 72 minutes, until an administrator unlocks it. An automatic lock no longer signs anyone out or stops their devices, temporary credentials, SFTP connections or links; an administrator's lock still does. The sign-in throttle counts a username per address. Behind a proxy not listed in TRUSTED_PROXIES every client has the proxy's address and shares one lock.

An administrator may make one change to another person's sign-in details (setting their password or making a reset link, resetting their second factor, changing their email address, adding an SSH key) per account in 14 days. A second one within that time is held for another administrator's approval and expires after 7 days. The approver must be independent of the change: not the one who asked nor the account's owner, not one who made the other an administrator, directly or through administrators they made, not one who changed that account's sign-in details in the 14 days before, and an administrator for at least 14 days (those from before 0.33.0 count as such). With no such administrator the change is refused (409), and the server's operator can make it from the host with python dockvault.py accounts. A user given the permission to manage users may make a first change to an ordinary user's account; a second one within 14 days is refused (409). Users are told in the app, and by email when email is set up, of every change an administrator makes to their account, lock, activation or role, and every other administrator is told when an account becomes an administrator.

Only for a deployment whose TRUSTED_PROXIES holds a range that contains the Docker network's gateway, such as the 172.16.0.0/12 that .env.example used to suggest: compare that line of .env with the gateway that docker network inspect dockvault-vault_vault-network shows. python dockvault.py update checks it before the upgrade only when the tool itself is 0.33.1 or later (update the checkout first: git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1; an older tool does not check). From 0.33.1 a range no longer trusts the gateway: connections Docker relays to the published port (IPv6 clients, clients on the Docker host, on Docker Desktop every client) are recorded as the gateway and their X-Forwarded-For is ignored. A reverse proxy on the Docker host connects from the gateway too, so after the upgrade all of its clients are recorded as the gateway and share one set of sign-in limits, and the web process says so at start. For such a proxy set TRUSTED_PROXIES=gateway and publish the web port on loopback only: WEB_BIND=127.0.0.1 with the secure compose file of 0.33.1 or later. An install that updates by pulling images keeps its old compose files, so edit its web port mapping to 127.0.0.1:<port>:8000 by hand, or update the checkout. A proxy container on the vault's network is not affected: list its address.

Before 0.33.1 every start of the web process granted each account that is not an administrator all of its role's default permissions again, so a default an administrator had revoked came back at the next restart. From 0.33.1 a start grants an account only defaults added in a later release, once, and a revoked default stays revoked. What an earlier restart granted back is still held and is not removed automatically: the check below lists each account and permission an administrator revoked that a restart then granted again, with the time of each, and so does, after the upgrade, the host tool of 0.33.1 or later: python dockvault.py accounts --action regranted-defaults once the checkout is updated (git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1; an older tool does not offer it), or docker exec vault python -m app.core.host_operator regranted-defaults (the container is vault-api in the split layout and the local trial). Revoke again, with the account's Permissions button on the Users page, what is still not wanted. A revocation the audit log no longer holds (a retention limit removed it) cannot be found. After a rollback to 0.33.0 the old start returns and grants revoked defaults again.
conditions.detect: WITH rev AS (SELECT a.resource_id AS user_id, g.grp, max(a.timestamp) AS revoked_at FROM audit_logs a CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(a.details::jsonb -> 'revoked_groups') = 'array' THEN a.details::jsonb -> 'revoked_groups' ELSE jsonb_build_array(a.details::jsonb ->> 'endpoint_group') END) AS g(grp) WHERE a.action = 'REVOKE_PERMISSION' AND a.status = 'success' GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT u.username, p.endpoint_group AS permission, rev.revoked_at, p.granted_at AS granted_again_at FROM rev JOIN user_endpoint_permissions p ON p.user_id::text = rev.user_id AND p.endpoint_group = rev.grp JOIN users u ON u.id = p.user_id WHERE p.granted_by IS NULL AND p.granted_at > rev.revoked_at ORDER BY u.username, p.endpoint_group

conditions.summary: Only for a deployment whose .env sets ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MINUTES=0 (the default is 15; the Settings page cannot set 0): look for that line in .env. The setting is read from .env, so there is no database check, and python dockvault.py update names it before the upgrade only when the tool itself is 0.33.1 or later (update the checkout first: git pull, or git fetch --tags and git checkout v0.33.1; an older tool does not check). An automatic lock after failed sign-ins then lasts until an administrator clears it, and before 0.33.1 that held for administrators too, so every administrator could be locked out for good. From 0.33.1 an administrator's automatic lock has an end, including one that 0.33.0 armed and is already in place: a lock on sign-ins from one address ends after 15 minutes, a pause on sign-ins from every address once its count has also lost a failure (72 minutes with the default settings). A lock with no end that a release before 0.33.0 armed is recorded like one an administrator set and stays, as other accounts' automatic locks do, until cleared from the host with the tool of 0.33.1 or later: python dockvault.py accounts --action unlock, or docker exec vault python -m app.core.host_operator unlock --username NAME --confirm-username NAME (the container is vault-api in the split layout and the local trial). With that setting, locking a name shows whether it is an administrator's (its lock ends).

From 0.33.1 the web and SFTP processes read the table data_requirements before they touch the database, and refuse to start when a newer release has marked the data as needing a newer version; the log names what changed and how to undo it with that release. ALLOW_START_ON_NEWER_DATA=true in .env starts them anyway, on data they cannot fully read. No release writes such a mark yet. 0.33.0 and earlier do not read the table, so a rollback to one of them is not protected by it; before a downgrade, python dockvault.py update from 0.33.1 on asks the running version what stands in the way, when that version offers the check.

waivers.reason: Floor release. Reachable only by a fresh deploy and restore-from-backup, not by an in-place upgrade from 0.16.1 (see the blocked 0.16.1 -> 0.17.0 edge). This is the minimum supported version; every release below it is end-of-life and insecure.
